Over the past week I formalized Terence Tao's Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values (arXiv:1909.03562, 2019; published in Forum of Mathematics, Pi, 2022) in Lean 4 + Mathlib. Public repo:

https://github.com/gotrevor/tao-collatz

Two headline theorems:

  • TaoCollatz.tao_collatz - Theorem 1.3: for any f : ℕ → ℝ with f N → ∞, almost all N (in logarithmic density) satisfy Colmin N < f N.
  • TaoCollatz.tao_collatz_quantitative - Theorem 3.1 (Colmin form): the log-probability that Colmin N ≤ N₀ on [1, x] is at least 1 - C/(log N₀)^c.

This is an AI-authored formalization. It was built using Claude Code (Anthropic Opus 4.8 & Fable 5) plus a custom autonomous "treadmill" grind harness.

Review surface:

  • The leanprover/comparator harness in CI rebuilds the headline statements from scratch over plain Mathlib, and replays the proofs through both the Lean kernel and the independent nanoda kernel.
  • The human audit surface is one small file: Comparator/TaoCollatz/Challenge.lean. The residual trust is exactly: "do these definitions faithfully capture the paper's claims."

Congratulations (although I should say that I did not independently check your work with comparator yet as I am away from my unix machine until the weekend). Thanks especially for the formalization.yaml and comparator files.

Nice!

If you want to make the statement closer to Mathlib-style: posInterval x is written in Mathlib as Finset.Icc 1 x.

Just one clarification question to make sure I correctly interpret the result...

If I plug the inverse Ackermann function for f,

Filter.Tendsto f Filter.atTop Filter.atTop

is satisfied, right?

Thanks Martin for clearing warnings in the repo: https://github.com/gotrevor/tao-collatz/pull/1

Floris van Doorn said:

Nice!

If you want to make the statement closer to Mathlib-style: posInterval x is written in Mathlib as Finset.Icc 1 x.

Thanks, Floris, this is clearly better. Implemented and merged: https://github.com/gotrevor/tao-collatz/pull/2
As for tao_collatz_quantitative are the numbers c and C known? I have hard time retrieving their values from the proof.

c≤1/(640,000,000⋅ln⁡2)≈2.25×10−9c \le 1/(640{,}000{,}000 \cdot \ln 2) \approx 2.25 \times 10^{-9}c≤1/(640,000,000⋅ln2)≈2.25×10−9 (a min; I traced one branch). Exists is a Prop, so the witness can't be projected out. It's a hand-read of ~8 obtain/refine layers.

CCC I couldn't get. One step takes its threshold from a bare limit, throwing away a rate that's elementary to supply, so there's no upper bound to read off. Nothing in Tao's argument is non-constructive; the qualitative statement just never needed the rate. It wouldn't be small anyway, since the witness carries 40d40^{\mathfrak{d}}40d with d≈3×107\mathfrak{d} \approx 3 \times 10^{7}d≈3×107.

Trace and refs: https://github.com/gotrevor/tao-collatz/pull/6. AFAIK the values aren't published: Tao says the methods are effective but he never computed them, and MO 341570 has been open since 2019. I'm going to try pinning ccc in Lean, and optimistically CCC. I'll follow up in the PR.

I think if nothing else, getting the effective constants would be good (cf https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/01/15/the-integrated-explicit-analytic-number-theory-network/, though it's not material for that)

Martin Dvořák said:

As for tao_collatz_quantitative are the numbers c and C known? I have hard time retrieving their values from the proof.

Here's a fully explicit version of Tao's quantitative theorem:

noncomputable def cTao : ℝ := 1 / (640_000_000 * Real.log 2)  -- ≈ 2.254 × 10⁻⁹
noncomputable def CTao : ℝ := (hyperoperation 4 10 63 : ℝ)  -- 10 ↑↑ 63
theorem tao_collatz_quantitative_fully_explicit :
    ∀ N₀ x : ℕ, 2 ≤ N₀ → 2 ≤ x →
      1 - CTao / (Real.log N₀) ^ cTao ≤ logProb {N | colMin N ≤ N₀} (Finset.Icc 1 x)

See PR #10.

I have not merged this. The result itself is checked, which you can see via the CI checks on the PR. My hesitation is architectural. Making every hidden constant and cutoff explicit required threading bookkeeping through 22 existing proof files. That's over 9,000 new lines. Many results now have _core, _atCX, _atC, and _explicit layers. This improves auditability of the constants, but makes an already machine-heavy proof substantially harder to read and navigate. The complexity was only around big C. The value for little c fell out rather straightforwardly.

I am considering whether to leave this as a separate audit artifact, reorganize the bookkeeping into companion modules, or accept that readability is not especially important for this part of the formalization.

Trevor Morris said:

I am considering whether to leave this as a separate audit artifact, reorganize the bookkeeping into companion modules, or accept that readability is not especially important for this part of the formalization.

I am quite surprised by this: are you suggesting that humans will be interested in reading AI-generated code which doesn't have explicit constants, but will not want to read AI-generated code which makes the constants explicit? You think the bar is "somewhere in the middle"? In my experience you want to avoid reading AI-generated code essentially always, unless you really want to see what went into it and then you bite the bullet and read it whatever it says.

Kevin Buzzard said:

In my experience you want to avoid reading AI-generated code essentially always

I agree, humans should avoid reading slop, but readability is still important for other LLMs. If another AI wants to build on this project, having a cleaner proof could make it easier to digest and find what it needs.

Personally, I'd just put the _explicit results into a separate folder, and explain in readme.md the rationale behind the split.

Yes, I am suggesting there is a bar "somewhere in the middle". I completely agree with Jack about machine readers, too.

The working agreement with the AIs was to stay close to the blueprint, which stays close to the paper. Every numbered claim in the paper (24: 3 theorems, 8 propositions, 12 lemmas, 1 corollary) has a blueprint node carrying its paper number in the title, with its Lean statement linked; in §7 it's one node per lemma. Where a Lean statement deliberately deviates from the paper's display, the node says so and why (e.g. Lemma 7.9 is pinned at e2εe^{2\varepsilon}e2ε where the paper states eεe^{\varepsilon}eε).

A few times, the AIs claimed to have found small errors in the paper's proofs. Those claims are recorded in the blueprint nodes and judge logs, and are still verifiable against the code as built - in fact, this month's v6 and v7 revisions of the paper already fix two of them. Once the code gets shuffled more, that kind of investigation gets harder.

So: is the human interface here just the Comparator, or is it the blueprint and the numbered claims too? I think it's both, and that's the bar I mean. Comparator certifies that the theorems hold; the structured engine preserves why - and the why is what you mine when checking errata claims or tightening the math (say, bringing the tower behind CCC down from 10↑↑6310\uparrow\uparrow 6310↑↑63). The less jumbled the Lean code, the easier it is to recognize it as faithful to the paper and to extend its logic.

Trevor Morris said:

The less jumbled the Lean code, the easier it is to recognize it as faithful to the paper and to extend its logic.

If there's a blueprint then the humans are going to read that. Most people are never going to read Lean code whatever it looks like. Who exactly are you catering for here? Perhaps we're talking at cross purposes.

I don't think we're at cross purposes, more that I'm finding my bearings in a foreign land, and I appreciate the engagement.

A parallel from my day job: I used to be a stickler for well-organized, legible Terraform. Now I care very little about the code, only that the plan is correct. I trust an AI could refactor it for clarity whenever I want, and I've yet to want to.

I merged #10.

I love reading Lean code that is well-organized and elegant. As for papers/blueprints, I hate reading them 100% of the time.
